title: Glowing Moss Slows Soil Erosion on Fictional Island of Verenta
question: How many soil plots were monitored in the study?
text:
Researchers at the (fictional) Halvorsen Institute of Coastal Ecology report that a bioluminescent moss, Luminobryum verentae, reduces soil erosion on hillside plots of the fictional island of Verenta.

The team monitored 48 soil plots over two years. Half of the plots were seeded with the moss and half were left bare as controls. Seeded plots lost an average of 31 percent less soil during heavy rainfall events than control plots. The moss formed a dense mat within five months, and its root-like rhizoids bound loose topsoil together.

Lead author Dr. Imra Coltrane said the moss could offer a low-cost way to stabilise slopes after wildfires. "It grows quickly, needs no irrigation, and it happens to glow faintly at night, which made it easy for volunteers to map," she said.

The authors caution that the study was conducted on a single island with a mild climate, and the two-year period included an unusually dry season, which may have reduced the number of extreme rainfall events. They also note that the moss's effect on native seedlings was not measured. Further trials on other islands and over longer periods are planned.

The study was funded by the Verenta Land Trust and published in the Journal of Imaginary Coastal Science.

title: Fictional Sleep Tonic Shows Modest Benefit in Small Trial
question: What was the name of the tonic tested in the trial?
text:
A small randomized trial at the (fictional) Brightwater Sleep Clinic found that an herbal tonic called Somnaril modestly improved self-reported sleep quality in adults with mild insomnia.

Sixty participants were randomly assigned to drink either Somnaril or a taste-matched placebo every evening for four weeks. Participants who received Somnaril reported falling asleep 9 minutes faster on average than those receiving placebo. Total sleep time did not differ meaningfully between groups. No serious adverse events were reported, although four participants in the Somnaril group reported mild morning drowsiness.

"The effect is real but small," said principal investigator Dr. Oskar Nyberg-Lane. "People should not expect it to cure insomnia."

The researchers note several limitations. The trial was small and ran at a single clinic, outcomes were based on self-reported sleep diaries rather than laboratory measurements, and the four-week follow-up cannot reveal long-term effects. The trial was partly funded by the company that manufactures Somnaril.

The findings were published in the fictional Annals of Restful Medicine.

title: Fictional Ceramic Coating Cuts Heat Loss in Prototype Kettles
question: By what percentage did the coating reduce heat loss?
text:
Engineers at the (fictional) Ostrava Applied Materials Lab have developed a ceramic coating that reduced heat loss from prototype electric kettles by 22 percent in laboratory tests.

The team coated 12 prototype kettles and compared them with 12 identical uncoated kettles. Water in coated kettles stayed above 70 degrees Celsius for an average of 41 minutes after boiling, compared with 29 minutes for uncoated kettles. The coating is made from a porous aluminosilicate foam that traps air in microscopic cells.

"This could save a little energy in every kitchen," said project lead Dr. Mirela Szabo. "But we still need to show that the coating survives years of daily use."

The researchers acknowledge that all tests were performed in a controlled laboratory, that coating durability over repeated heating cycles has not been tested beyond three months, and that manufacturing costs at scale are unknown.

The results appear in the fictional Bulletin of Household Engineering.
